senses.definition: (countable) Someone who likes to talk about other people's private or personal business.
examples: Be careful what you say to him: he’s a bit of a gossip.

quotes.text: A losing Gamester, who is obliged to drive into the City to dispose of a little South Sea Stock, gives the Hint there. The Gossips at Garraway’s have it in a Moment: At One it is buzz’d on Change, and the circulating Whisper in the Boxes interrupts the Play at Night.
quotes.reference: 1752, Arthur Murphy, The Gray’s Inn Journal, volume 1, number 11, page 73:

quotes.text: He was an arrant old gossip, too; for ever coming off in his canoe to the ships in the bay, and regaling their crews with choice little morsels of court scandal […]
quotes.reference: 1846, Herman Melville, “Sequel Containing the Story of Toby”, in Typee:

quotes.text: Alf could tell you about everybody on both sides of Main Street. He was a vicious male gossip, insatiably curious and vindictive without malice.
quotes.reference: 1952, John Steinbeck, chapter 48, in East of Eden, London: Heinemann, page 456:

senses.definition: (uncountable) Idle talk about someone’s private or personal matters, especially about someone not present.
examples: According to the latest gossip, their relationship is on the rocks.
I have a juicy piece of gossip to share with you.

quotes.text: […] the thing is certainly true. It is not a mere bit of gossip. We have it from Frederick himself.

quotes.text: The smaller a town the more richly it hums with gossip. There are no private affairs here. Gossip is the air we breathe.

(now only historical) A sponsor; a godfather or godmother; the godparent of one's child or godchild, or the parent of one's godchild.

quotes.text: ’tis not a maid, for she hath had gossips [i.e. she could not be a virgin, because she has children with godparents]

quotes.text: It seems, Miss, that if he stood not himself, or procur’d not Gossips for the Christening of the Children of his poorer Tenants, he always sent them a large rich Cake […]
